Anyway, I would be curious to check out this expansion just for

I'm curious as to how supply issues are dealt with. I assume it is the
usual situation as far as playtested experimental "expansions" are
concerned: everyone is given a complete "spoiler list" and then allowed
to bring as many proxies as they wish? If so, you have an ideal
situation: a new expansion with all the fun and added variety, unlimited
supply of "cards" for all, and none of the practical problems of supply
and demand that "fragmentation" creates. To argue on the basis of such
an example, you are only looking at one side of the picture. I hope you
don't think that I am adocating against further fragmentation simply
because I am some stuck-in-the-mud curmudgeon who despises variety,
novelty and innovation.

I sympathize with your interest in the Cappodocians. They certain seem
more interesting and more flexible than their dull-as-dirt Giovanni
replacements. (The Giovanni were an idea that seem to have been based on
an ethnic steriotype, which is always a bad start. The rigid nature of
the clan makes it hard for individual members to break the mold.)

Even if we were to add the Capodocians, do we really need the Mortis
discipline? My understanding is that some of the descendants of
Cappodocians, like the Harbingers of Skulls, practice Necromancy, which
has a new "Path of Mortuus" that somewhat mimics the powers of the Mortis
discipline. This being the case, is a new "Mortis" discipline really
needed? New disciplines are possibly a bigger fragmentation problem than
new clans are.

We already have 17 disciplines, and have not even begun to explore the
number of discipline combos that this makes possible. In WoD role playing
game this is not a problem because it is based around individual
characters which can be made as atypical as one likes. In V:tES one
typically needs at least two to four characters of similar focus to even
think of trying to make a deck around a particular discipline combo (I
have not seen anyone use Patrizia Giovanni or Mirembe Kabbada yet). But
there are 136 possible 2 discipline combos, 680 possible 3-discipline
combos, and 2380 possible 4-discipline combos (I hope I got that right).
But anyway that's alot of possibilities to be exploring -- ones that might
support strategies that are not currently workable. It seems to me that
introducing a whole new discipline into such a situation is an insult to
the enormous potential already present, especially since there is little
reason why new card concepts could not be introduced within the context of
the present discipline structure.

So, why waste an opportunity to expore a new discipline combo. If the
Cappodocians are to be introduced at some far distant date, should they
not have Fortitude, Auspex and Necromancy? If new "death magic" ideas are
to be introduced to the game, why not do it withing the context of
Necromancy? If you don't want the Giovanni using these special cards,
then print Necromancy cards that work well only in combination with
Fortitude or Auspex effects. If no suitable Auspex effects exist
currently for a combo you have in mind, then invent a new card.

If you introduce a new Mortis discipline with the Cappodocians, then
little is done to explore new pairings of old disciplins. We already have
a clan that combines Auspex and Fortitude. But if we give the modern
Cappodocians Necromancy, then Aus & Nec, and For & Nec, get combined for
the first time. This allows the exploration of new possibilities for
Necromancy, rather than leaving it stuck in a marginalized corner of the
game.

-- John Whelan

On Tue, 12 Sep 2000 inr...@my-deja.com wrote:

> my take on this is that new clans and disiplines are a good way to avoid

This is a point, and I was wondering when someone would mention it.
However, Vampire already has the equivalent of 39+ colors of mana, as
compared to Magic's 5. This is already a stabilizing factor, making it
rather difficult to print cards that will replace the entire set in one
go. The basic design is also a safeguard. That the game is based on
Vampires means that can always use MORE Vampires who will help make one's
decks more focussed and therefore more efficient, but that one does not
necessarily need BETTER Vampires. White Wolf realizes (hopefully) that
the problem with the marginal clans is that there were not enough of them,
not that they were not powerful enough on an individual basis. Hopefully
they realize that we can always use new vampires, and they need not be
more powerful than the ones that came before.

Question is: can there be too much of a good thing? Surely you realize
that making it difficult for White Wolf to Screw Things Up, also means
making it difficult for them to do lots of other things, like maybe Get
Things Right. It makes it harder to provide any service to existing
clans, or reward the interests and expectations of an increasingly
fragmented customer base. What if people stop buy fewer cards because
they are not as interested in the particular clans not currently being
serviced.

Fragmentation means that White Wolf can only service part of the game at
one time. The "good" news is that there is absolutely NO chance that the
Assamites, the Settites, the Giovanni, or the Ravnos will become "broken"
or overpowered because of the new Sabbat War cards. There is no chance
that old Clan-specific cards for Camarilla & Independents, Chimeristry
cards, Serpentis Cards, Necromancy cards, or Quietus cards will be
rendered obsolete. But if we really want to play it that safe, perhaps we
should do without expansions altogether.

> If
> the cards are play tested and balanced, then they can be integrated
> without causing all of the older cards to be useless, and further,
> generating renewed interest in the game (as well as renewed sales for
> White Wolf).

I don't think we need an expansion every year, though it certainly would
be nice to get a few promo vampires on a regular basis. New vampires with
new discipline combos will certainly create new opportunities to explore
"Cool Things tm" from the Jyhad set.

> gee, that didn't sound all that divisive. darn. still, better safe

their use by the Giovanni. Another option is combat cards that work
better if you are a non-acting minion (thus more usable in Auspex-using

How about printing alternate versions of earlier Thaumaturgy cards, in
which one gains damnation counters instead of paying blood costs (or some
similar trade-off), as defined by card text. This way we keep the
simplicity of a single discipline. The particular path or variant
followed by a minion will depend on the particular cards a Methuselah puts

counters" as part of their cost, then clearly the minion playing it is a

I don't believe there is a difference between the two. Helping a deck
type(s) become more efficient is the definition of a "better" card.
And that isn't just limited to the vampire card type. Any card
introduced in expansion, can impact gameplay and deck construction,
for better or worse. Dreams of the Sphinx (AH) comes to mind, as well
as Horrific Countenance (DS).

>the problem with the marginal clans is that there were not enough of them,
>not that they were not powerful enough on an individual basis. Hopefully
>they realize that we can always use new vampires, and they need not be
>more powerful than the ones that came before.

I guess I'm missing your definition of "power," as applied to a vamp.
I see five criteria for vamps: capacity, skills, base damage, base
bleed, and votes/title. Clan, skill, and title allow certain
strengths and vulnerabilities, as denoted in the library cards. All
of these criteria, when considered as a whole, fall short of measuring
power, as a vamp's power is still limited by hand size, library size,
commonality of criteria, game mechanic, library composition and
library order. Example: The 12 (or 13) Crypt Machine vamps (4-caps
with dom) are orders of magnitude more powerful than any collection of
Inner Circle vamps. Why? because I can guarantee that I'll start with
4 unique vamps in the crypt, that share a skill (dom), and can run a
library based on that skill.

>Question is: can there be too much of a good thing? Surely you realize

>making it difficult for them to do lots of other things, like maybe Get

>clans, or reward the interests and expectations of an increasingly
>fragmented customer base. What if people stop buy fewer cards because
>they are not as interested in the particular clans not currently being

The simple answer is: they're missing out. One of the main points of
this game, is that clan divisions are transparent, to the overall goal
of ousting one's prey. If a player does not understand this function,
they don't understand the game.

What you have hit on, is the notion that improper combinations of
clan, skill, function, and/or cost (in game terms) tend to fail
because they contrast against the core mechanics and dynamics. This
is a separate issue from fragmentation, though.

I'll use Eyes of the Dead (DS) and Deadliest Sin (AH or S?) as an
example.

EotD, requires a skill, and provides a function. DSin, a skillless
card, provides function equal to superior-skill EotD, plus extra
function not included in EotD, for the same cost.

This pair of cards is broken, because it reverses a core concept of
V:TES: skilled library cards should offer an advantage to unskilled
cards, either in cost or effect.

That's a blatant example, but several such mistakes, of varying
impact, reside in the existing expansion sets.

>
>Fragmentation means that White Wolf can only service part of the game at
>one time. The "good" news is that there is absolutely NO chance that the
>Assamites, the Settites, the Giovanni, or the Ravnos will become "broken"
>or overpowered because of the new Sabbat War cards. There is no chance
>that old Clan-specific cards for Camarilla & Independents, Chimeristry
>cards, Serpentis Cards, Necromancy cards, or Quietus cards will be
>rendered obsolete. But if we really want to play it that safe, perhaps we
>should do without expansions altogether.
>

Here, you're talking breadth of game, vs. scope of expansion.

Take the Camarilla vamps from Ancient Hearts, as an illustration.
(note: I am deliberately excluding Ravnos/Giovanni from this example).
It looks like valuable vamp slots were taken from the main clans of
the set (Assamite/Setite), to create "hook" vamps for Camarilla clans,
utilizing a combination of old and new skills. The result is a subset
of vampires that cannot use either Settite or Assamite cards, but
don't have the skills to really be useful in their designated clans.
Since the point of the expansion was to introduce two new clans, the
mis-clanned vampires are wasted card slots, from the scope of the
expansion, resulting in incomplete clans.

No, but you need to take that position to argue that Fragmentation does
not impact players, and reduce the amount of "usable" game material that
the average player will get from an average expansion.

> The thing is, if you continue to make the "General" expansions that you
> seem to advocate, where you have to have cards for all the clans that
> have gone before, everyone has to buy everything.

Why do you keep saying that I "seem" to advocate general expansions?

I have repeatedly stated that I advocate focussed expansions. I have
advocated that some clans and disciplines be left out entirely, and that
each expansion should focus on at most 7 clans and 10 disciplines (as the
original did). I am of the opinion that all sets after the first spread
themselves too thin and tried to do too much.

I recognize that, because of the level of fragmentation, hard choices must
be made. I have recommended that those hard choices be made, particularly
when an expansion is a "standalone" and intended to rake in new players.

> If I want all the
> Gangrel cards, I have to go and buy every expansion, because there are
> Gangrel cards in all of them.

Yes. That is one of the sad things about Fragmentation. There is no way
to avoid the possible consequences that customers will be lost. If a
focussed expansion is made, and it leaves out the Gangrel and some other
clans, then there is a chance that fans of the omitted clans will not buy
the new set, or not as much of it. In other words, part of White Wolf's
customer base is lost. This increases the chance that the expansion will
not turn a profit, which in turn increases the chance that there will
never be a "next expansion".

White Wolf's other option is to print cards for all clans and disciplines
in each set. That way, there is a "hook" for all the players. The
downside is that those who do buy the set will get minimal reward for
their money. Players may feel disatisfied that they spend a whole load of
money for a lesser quantity of cards they consider usable. White Wolf may
still lose customers.

So you see, the choice between focussed expansions and general expansions
is a lose-lose situation. There is no way to avoid the consequences of
fragmentation, and one can only hope that the demand for the game is
sufficient to support it in spite of these problems.

Between the two, I advocate focussed expansions, because I feel these are
better for hooking in new players.

> With the more focused expansions that a number of people are talking
> about,

....people like me, you mean. As I recall, I was the one who first
brought up the issue by advocating for them, and so started this whole
discussion.

> each with its own distinct task to fulfil, you can be a V:TES
> fanatic, get lots of Gangrel cards but rarely feel compelled to go out
> and buy boosters for another expansion because some of your essential
> cards are in it.

This is great for the interests of the particular player, but bad for
White Wolf's profits. I'm not concerned about White Wolf's profits,
except for the consideration that if they don't get adequate profits,
neither do we get any further expansions. Is the customer base
sufficiently large that WW can afford to target an expansion at only a
fraction of it? I hope so, because there isn't much of a choice.

Once again!: I am not saying this to argue against focussed expansions,
which I feel are the better way to go (even from the POV of White Wolf's
profits). I am merely pointing out that you cannot avoid facing
consequences of fragmentation no matter how you do things. The moral of
the story: don't increase fragmentation.

-- John Whelan

Get a clan up to a good level, then let it go free. You then don't need
to go back and add new cards, because it can already fight for itself.

>There is no way
>to avoid the possible consequences that customers will be lost. If a
>focussed expansion is made, and it leaves out the Gangrel and some other

>customer base is lost. This increases the chance that the expansion will
>not turn a profit, which in turn increases the chance that there will

If you make it a small expansion, on a small print-run, you have:

1) Fewer designers involved - less money spent on work-force, and the WW
staff can be off writing for V:tM or M:tA or whatever.

2) Fewer pieces of original artwork to commission or licence.

3) Less card stock to buy - paper is expensive

4) Less packaging to print

5) Less packing to get done

6) Less shipping to pay

etc. etc. etc.

Let's just say, for the sake of argument, that V:TES had 1000 cards
printed for it. (Just picking very low numbers to keep it manageable,
not for any real reason.)

Now, we come and print our new expansion, Ancient Sovereigns. We only
decide to print 300 cards for it, meaning:

- Well, that's the artists gone down to three-tenths of the original
cost, assuming we commission along a similar pattern of
expensive/inexpensive (relatively) artists.

- We only have to buy three sheets of paper instead of ten (100 cards
per sheet, say).

- We employed three designers for V:TES, but we decide to only employ 1
for this set. Not a three-tenths reduction, but a significant reduction
by two-thirds.

- We only have to ship three tenths as many boxes of cards.

Now, not everything will reduce in price by three-tenths, of course not.
You need at least one designer, so you can't go down to three-tenths.
The cost of paying for a courier or posting a package etc. will reduce,
but they'll have a flat rate to work from, too. Similarly, you'll have
to pay for a certain amount of the printing press - you can't just print
1 card and pay only for the card, since you have to pay for their time
etc. as well.

But, costs come down.

And if you look at V:TES vs Ancient Hearts, you can see that they
compensate for that too. In Britain, Ancient Hearts was normally sold
for around 1.80GBP a booster, which works out to about 15 pence a card.
(About 3 dollars, or 25 cents a card.) The wraps suggest that it was
$2.25 in the US, but I assume each state's sales tax has to be put on
top, whereas Britain already has VAT in the price. But you get the idea
as to price.

If I can just find a pack of V:TES around, it was sold at around 6.50
when it came out here, around 10 dollars. 76 cards and a rulebook.
Well, let's exclude the rulebook, as it's not really what people buy it
for once they have one or two. It. was sold, according to the box, at
$8.95 in the US. That makes each of the 76 cards significantly cheaper.
Taking it in British prices, that works out to about 8 pence a card.
(12 cents.)

Or in US prices direct, excluding sales tax, that gives us 18.75 cents a
card in AH, but only 11.78 cents a card in V:TES.

By way of simple comparison, to get 76 Ancient Hearts cards, you have to
buy six and a third AH boosters. (76/12) That would cost you $14.25,
significantly more than the same in V:TES.

But Ancient Hearts still sells, doesn't it? A lot of people find it
hard to get, as they do with Sabbat (which was $3.95 a pack for 28
cards, about 14 cents a card, or about $10.72 a starter).

These weren't printed on the same scale as V:TES or Jyhad, but they do
still tick a profit. (Except for Wizards monumentally cocking up
Sabbat.) No, they may not be as profitable as V:TES, but that isn't the
only thing to consider.

A company that doesn't print new games etc., will end up slipping out of
the forefront of the market. They lose market share, as everyone has
already bought what they want of their old stock. So, just printing a
new expansion, even if it is slightly less profitable than it could be,
can be a perfectly good thing to do. And I know, for myself, that it
brought both Wizards of the Coast and White Wolf to my attention
whereas, at the time, I was mostly playing things like AD&D, Decipher
card games (Star Trek) and a number of war games like Diplomacy.

How much have I spent on White Wolf products since? A lot, I'd
certainly say. I have each of the basic books for V:tM, Mage, Werewolf,
Wraith (all 2nd) and Changeling (1st). I have a number of clan books
for V:tM, a copy of V:tM 3rd, the players guide (2nd), the story-tellers
guide (1st), one of the Sabbat guides (2nd), a number of clan novels, a
copy of "Truth Until Paradox" (which is really quite cool), a copy of
Werewolf's Mind's Eye rules and so on. I keep toying with buying Mage:
Sorcerer's Crusade, but haven't done so yet. Just how much of that
would I have spent had White Wolf helped WotC develop Jyhad? A damn
sight less, I can be certain. These are hidden profits that a company
cannot track. All the sales tell you is that I went out and bought a
lot of White Wolf stuff - which can be attributed to the fact that White
Wolf spent time and money with WotC developing a game. White Wolf could
only, seriously, attribute those profits to the success of their lines,
when they should in fact be partially attributed to the success of
V:TES.

How *do* you get new players to play the game? Well, a new expansion,
or a publicity stunt, promo cards etc. will help. One of the best
options is to keep people playing it, so that they introduce people to
it. Dropping new cards into the game helps liven things up.

I have no idea, but I would certainly say that the answer was "More than
0", how many players were introduced to the game via friends. And how
many of those friends were still playing V:TES because they had plenty
of new ideas and creativity to play with from Dark Sovereigns, or
Ancient Hearts? I would say more than 0. So, printing those later
expansions brings more sales to V:TES - again, hidden profits, where
Dark Sovereigns makes another product more profitable.

And then there's PR. White Wolf have, to my mind, got some of the best
public relations of any games company in the world, at the moment. Yes,
they're there to make a profit. Yes, bills need to be paid. But, yes,
they do actually interact with their customers, listening to them,
talking to them, printing some of the products their customers actually
want, rather than only those things that will be most profitable. That
sort of things create brand loyalty.

Similarly, O'Reilly Associates print a great deal of very useful
computer books, with excellent in-depth treatment of many subjects.
They don't just print the most profitable books, but spend time and
money on more minority interests. They also invest a great deal of
time, money and effort investing back into the Perl community, which was
one of their greatest assets. It's created phenomenal brand loyalty.
If I know there is an O'Reilly on a specific subject, I can be quite
happy buying it without having done much more than read a sample on-line
and flicked through it in the shops, and I know for certain I'm not the
only person who does that. A number of the local book shops in Britain
have a computer section, ranging over a number of shelves. Some of the
bigger ones split it up into things like "Networking", "Programming
Languages", "General", "Operating Systems". We have an "O'Reilly"
section too, in two of the large chain book-shops (Waterstones, as it
happens).

The amount of direct profit you make isn't always as important as the
amount of good-will you generate, at the same time. If you can get a
reputation for making quality, giving customers what they want *and*
keeping it affordable, not pumping out trash, not just trying to milk
customers for money, that sort of thing can pay off in spades - and that
certainly seems to be where White Wolf try and capitalise.

Just pumping out another expansion, with the same old clans, with the
same old cards etc., can be viewed as just another expansion, with
nothing new to add. A lot of people object to having to buy all the
V:TES dross that's in Sabbat. Why do I need another 15 Magnums, when I
already had 7 googolplex of them from V:TES?

>White Wolf's other option is to print cards for all clans and disciplines
>in each set. That way, there is a "hook" for all the players. The
>downside is that those who do buy the set will get minimal reward for
>their money.

Exactly.

> Players may feel disatisfied that they spend a whole load of
>money for a lesser quantity of cards they consider usable. White Wolf may
>still lose customers.

They would also lose considerable reputation, I feel. And reputation is
their second strongest asset. (A lot of high quality games is their
strongest asset.)

>So you see, the choice between focussed expansions and general expansions
>is a lose-lose situation.

So we should never print any more cards then? If it's lose-lose, as you
suggest, they should just not bother?

I assert that the situation isn't lose-lose. At least one of the
options is simply "Not win as much", rather than "Lose".

>> With the more focused expansions that a number of people are talking
>> about,
>
>....people like me, you mean. As I recall, I was the one who first
>brought up the issue by advocating for them, and so started this whole
>discussion.

You spent half of your rebuttal of one of my posts talking about adding
one card per clan - which was entirely contrary to the spirit of focus I
was advocating.

>> each with its own distinct task to fulfil, you can be a V:TES
>> fanatic, get lots of Gangrel cards but rarely feel compelled to go out
>> and buy boosters for another expansion because some of your essential
>> cards are in it.
>
>This is great for the interests of the particular player, but bad for
>White Wolf's profits.

I assert that not exploiting players is of benefit to their profits -
and a small profit for the game is better than no profit for not
printing for it.

>I'm not concerned about White Wolf's profits,
>except for the consideration that if they don't get adequate profits,
>neither do we get any further expansions. Is the customer base
>sufficiently large that WW can afford to target an expansion at only a
>fraction of it?

At the moment? Possibly not. That's why White Wolf have been investing
time, money and effort into expanding the player base. The pre-con
starters are a huge benefit. The play-mat is also great. From the
sound of things, one of the useful things in the new rules book will be
links to the existing community, so that people don't pick up the game,
play in isolation and never try again - they have web resources,
newsgroups etc. to capitalise upon.

accept my word for it when I say (at least half a dozen times now) that I
advocate focussed expansions, not "general" ones that attempt to service all
clans and disciplines..

>>I have repeatedly stated that I advocate focussed expansions. I have
>>advocated that some clans and disciplines be left out entirely,
>

Yes, I said that. I said it because 1) it is true, and 2) because it was part
of my argument concerning inevitable consequences of fragmentation. It was not
part of any argument supporting unfocussed "general" expansions (as I have
already clarified more than once).

I'm sure you agree with me that the proposition is TRUE (ie. giving more to
your clans of focus necessarily means giving less to other clans). So why are
you insisting that this proposition leads to a conclusion other than the one I
am presenting? Especially since it is a conclusion you don't agree with

I merely said that it was ONE of the (potential) "sad things" about
Fragmentation. It applies to unfocussed expansions that attempt to service all
clans/disciplines. What you just mentioned is the OTHER "sad thing" about
Fragmentation. It applies to focussed expansions that focus on some
clans/disciplines and leave out others.

An expansion must be either focussed or unfocussed. My arguments have
addressed both possibilities. My thesis is that negative consequences are
unavoidable no matter what the style of the expansion. My arguments that apply
to "general" expansions are not intended to argue against "general" expansions
(although, incidentally, I am not in favor of such). My arguments that apply
to "focussed" expansions are not indended as arguments against focussed
expansions (in fact I support such). My thesis (for the umpteenth time) is
that Fragmentation has negative consequences, which cannot be avoided.

>Get a clan up to a good level, then let it go free. You then don't need
>to go back and add new cards, because it can already fight for itself.

You made this point before. I have already responded to it a previous post.
The next paragraph was my previous response, verbatim..

"You really think that is possible ... print a clan once and have the bases
covered forever? So that it will never again need to be expanded? So that the
people who play that clan will not want it to be expanded? So that they will
not be disappointed with the latest expansion that does not add materials for

playing it, then I'm sure this won't be a problem, but in that case why bother

clans is at all successful, then White Wolf has succeeded in further
fragmenting the demands of its available players, such that it will be harder

Let me add something to what I said previously. There is nothing wrong with
the level any of the current clans are at, except that it is less than other
clans. All clans are playable. They are just less playable than clans that

>If you make it a small expansion, on a small print-run, you have:

James, you get so involved with the little details that you cannot see the
forest for the trees. Everything you have written below is irrelevant to the
broad issue being discussed. Smaller expansions and smaller print runs are not
at issue here. Such strategies of production and release may be important in
and of themselves, maximizing profit potential is correctly done. But they
cannot alter the basic marketting fact that fewer customers (or fewer satisfied
customers) PER CARD is a bad thing, no matter how those cards are packaged, or
in what sort of expansions they are organized.

By "a small expansion", I presume you mean fewer total card varieties per
expansion. By "a small print run", I presume you mean fewer of each card is
printed.

I will address the "smaller print run" issue first. In this, you only save on
shipping, packaging, and the like. You do not save on design, development,
artwork, etc. Because of this, a smaller print run is less efficient in terms
of cost per card, and these costs must be passed on to the customer in order to
make a profit. It is always more efficient to make a larger print run --
provided of course that one can find sufficient customers for the product.
There is no way around this. If you concede that Fragmentation forces WW to
make smaller print runs (as would be the case if each expansion were targetted
at a subsection or "fragment" of its customer base), then you necessarily
concede that it has negative consequences for either customer costs or company
profits (most likely both).

In a "small expansion", your savings are across the board, but this will not
improve profits. Players are not likely to make up for your printing fewer
cards by buying more of each. Unfortunately, "small expansions" don't help
with the problem of fragmentation at all. It is the very nature of
Fragmentation that MORE cards (not less) are necessary to service the entire
game. We have already established that the current level of fragmentation is
such that a DS/AH-sized expansion of say 180 cards is inadequate to service the
entire game, and should therefore try to service only a fraction of available
clans/disciplines in order to maintain adequate focus. So, are you NOW
suggesting that expansions should be even smaller than 180 cards? If so, they
will either have to sacrifice focus, or become even MORE specialized, even
narrower in scope, than a 180-card expansion would have to be. It appears you
are advocating increased specialization. In other words, each expansion will
be targetted at an even SMALLER subsection of the V:tES community (possibly
going as far as a mini-expansion for each clan?). That's fine, but that
necessarily means that each expansion MUST have a smaller print run. For the
consequences of a smaller print run, see previous paragraph. Essentially this
is a marketing issue. Lets take, hypothetically, a huge expansion of 1300
cards which has something for everyone and is vast and broad enough to service
the entire scope of the game. Do you market it as a single expansion to the
whole community and risk the disatisfaction by requiring your customers to pay
for cards they don't want? Or do you divide it up into 13 different
mini-expansions of 100 cards each (each perhaps focussed on a separate clan),
and target each expansion at a fraction (or "fragment") of the total customer
base? I agree that the second option (or a less extreme variation of it) is
the better strategy, but it still has undesirable consequences .... the
consequences of Fragmentation.

For some strange reason, you think I have taken a position against further

Best I can tell, you are trying to convince me that it doesn't matter if
Fragmentation is increased, because negative consequences like reduced profit

If fragmentation is increased, other factors may compensate, yes. But things

<snip OReilly example>

>The amount of direct profit you make isn't always as important as the
>amount of good-will you generate, at the same time. If you can get a

>keeping it affordable, not pumping out trash, not just trying to milk
>customers for money, that sort of thing can pay off in spades - and that

I'm certainly glad to hear that. Can we get back to the point? Or are you
conceding that I am right about Fragmentation's negative consequences, but that
it does not matter because their are other considerations besides direct
profit? Yes, I agree that other factors besides fragmentation affect a game's
success. An unfragmented game can fail, for instance, because it is total
crap.

I certainly hope that White Wolf will, as you say "give customers what they
want *and* keep it affordable". My argument about fragmentation is that this
makes it increasingly difficult for them to do both.

>Just pumping out another expansion, with the same old clans, with the
>same old cards etc., can be viewed as just another expansion, with
>nothing new to add. A lot of people object to having to buy all the
>V:TES dross that's in Sabbat. Why do I need another 15 Magnums, when I
>already had 7 googolplex of them from V:TES?

WHOAH! Stop right there! What is this "same old clans -- same old cards"
nonsense? "Same old clans" is one thing. "Same old cards" is something else
entirely. The two issues have ABSOLUTELY NOTHING to do with each other.
Nobody -- and certainly not me -- is advocating in favor of printing "same old
cards". This is unrelated to anything I ever said or advocated.

Neither do these concepts go together historically. Sabbat was the first
expansion to feature "same old cards" ... yet this same set featured not a
single vampire for the "same old clans" of earlier sets.

Do you really think it is impossible to add exciting new stuff to the game
without fragmenting the game structure? Do you really feel that the best way
to revitalize the game is to print alot of new-clan-specific and
new-discipline-specific resources that no vampires in ANY of the old clans can
use AT ALL. Would it not be better to print cards that can be used by at least
SOME of the already-existing vampires?

I also want to remind you that my primary fragmentation concern is disciplines,
not clans. I would guess that a new clan with a new discipline has at least 3
times the fragmentation effect as a new clan featuring older disciplines. Even
at inferior, a discipline is a more important resource-access that a clan
designation. My worry about "new clans" is based on the knowledge that almost
all additional bloodlines or clans in the WoD are given their own special
discipline.

<snip>

>> Players may feel disatisfied that they spend a whole load of
>>money for a lesser quantity of cards they consider usable. White Wolf may
>>still lose customers.
>They would also lose considerable reputation, I feel. And reputation is
>their second strongest asset. (A lot of high quality games is their
>strongest asset.)

You do not imagine you are arguing with me here, I hope. Let me remind you
once again that I am in favor of focussed expansions -- specifically stated
before you first posted on this issue, and many times since..

<snip>

> So we should never print any more cards then? If it's lose-lose, as you
> suggest, they should just not bother?

You know well enough that that is not my point, because I have already stated
what my point is a dozen times.

I argued that we should not should not add new clans & disciplines because it
increases the fragmentation problem. You responded that that is not true, and
that fragmentation problems do not apply if expansions are "done right" (ie.
sufficiently focussed). Your view was that since fragmentation problems could
be avoided, we could safely add new clans and disciplines and not worry about
the consequences. I pointed out that fragmentation problems DO apply, even to
focussed expansions.

And what was the conclusion of my argument? Why don't I make it easier and
turn it into a multiple choice question. Which of the following is John
Whelan's thesis:

(A) We should make general expansions, not focussed ones.
(B) We should make focussed expansions, not general ones
(C) We should give up and not make any more expansions at all.
(D) We should not increase fragmentation by adding new clans with new
disciplines.

OK. Times up! The correct answer is (D). All the other answers are incorrect
(though I agree with (B) it does not derive from my fragmentation argument).
And if you come up with any other conclusions of your own devising, I would
appreciate if you not attribute them to me.

> I assert that the situation isn't lose-lose. At least one of the
> options is simply "Not win as much", rather than "Lose".

YES! YES! That is PRECISELY why I am in FAVOR os FOCUSSED expansions. The
"lose-lose" situation is indended to apply ONLY to the fragmentation problem...
meaning that the negative consequences of Fragmentation cannot be avoided. It
does not extend beyond that consideration. My thesis is (i repeat i repeat i
repeat) that the negative consequences of Fragmentation apply to both types of
expansions. The reference to a "lose-lose situation" applies only to
consequences of Fragmentation. There are other considerations, some of which
(I agree) favor focussed expansions, which is why I support focussed
expansions.

<snip>

>You spent half of your rebuttal of one of my posts talking about adding
>one card per clan - which was entirely contrary to the spirit of focus I
>was advocating.

I have already clarified this issue. You posted your example to rebut my claim
that problems associated with fragmentation were unavoidable. I countered by
showing that you example still suffered from problems associated with
fragmentation. Fragmentation forces an expansion to either give each clan or
discipline very little OR leave out clans / disciplines altogether. .

I put alot of work and took great pains to clarify my position. Now you enter
the debate again, making the same accusations. I find this very rude. You do
not have the right to tell me what my opinions are. Disagree if you must, but
disagree with the position I present, not with another of your own devising.

<snip>

>I assert that not exploiting players is of benefit to their profits -
>and a small profit for the game is better than no profit for not
>printing for it.

The more we avoid increasing the Fragmentation problem, the less we are forced
to choose between the lesser of evils. Don't you get it? I am arguing for
NOT increasing the fragmentation problem. I am NOT arguing that any one option
for coping with the problem is necessarily better than any other. I tend to
believe that focussed expansions are preferable, but that is a side issue.

<snip>

>That's why White Wolf have been investing
>time, money and effort into expanding the player base. The pre-con
>starters are a huge benefit. The play-mat is also great. From the
>sound of things, one of the useful things in the new rules book will be
>links to the existing community, so that people don't pick up the game,
>play in isolation and never try again - they have web resources,
>newsgroups etc. to capitalise upon.

These are certainly good things. If they are successful in increasing the
player base, then this may give the game sufficient strength cope with the
fragmentation level -- perhaps even a greater fragmentation level that exists
currently.

I would not (in the very long run -- provided the game is successful enough to
support it) be averse to new clans that explore new combos of old disciplines.
I have no interest in adding new disciplines at all -- it seems a total waste
to me --, but perhaps the game would survive IF the player base was
sufficiently large and healthy.

However fragmentation, once increased, becomes a permanent issue. If business
or popularity should slow down for any reason, greater fragmentation increases
the chance that the game will not survive at all.

-- John Whelan

That's very odd. Unlike your previous example, Eyes of the Dead vs.
The Deadliest Sin, nonFree-Kewl RC is clearly _not_ better as its one
blood cost is a drawback not present in Kine RC. In fact, I doubt it
would be very popular at all, as the drain on the political vampires would
constrain other tactics (such as running an effective Fifth Tradition/
Minion Tap combo) more than the one extra pool burnt by the victims
would be worth.

I agree with some of your original complaints. But sometimes this sort
of thing happens because the designers need to correct problems with
the game. For instance, Eyes of the Dead was ridiculous. One or two
intercept IF the vampire had Necromancy IF the acting minion was
diablerizing one of your vampires? Now there's a card that's redraw
meat every time I have the misfortune to draw it. The last thing I want
is for the designers to feel like they need to stick a drawback in every
card that at least encompasses that paltry functionality. As it turns out,
even The Deadliest Sin is so specialized that it's unlikely to be used
much, despite its no-discipline requirement and the other advantages
over Eyes of the Dead. In general, yes, cards should be a matter of
tradeoffs between one another so the choice between them is a
matter of skill, not just owning more copies of a "better" card. But
if they design a real clinker and the game needs a better version, it's
best to just admit the mistake and design the "better" card.

As for vampires, I think LSJ is admitting that more vampires are
just plain better for a clan. However, that doesn't mean that each
individual vampire is better than previous vampires (except previous
vampires that were badly designed, similar to bad library cards).
And that seems that the correct thing to do to me.

Fred
